title: Explain method overriding in depth — rules, covariant return types, access-modifier rules, exception rules, and use cases.
shortTitle: Method overriding in depth — rules, covariant returns, access modifiers, exceptions, use cases

s1_definition.profdef: Method overriding occurs when a child class provides a SPECIFIC implementation for a method already defined in its parent class. The overriding method must have the SAME name, SAME parameter list, and a COMPATIBLE return type. Five rules govern overriding: (1) COVARIANT RETURN — the return type can be the same OR a subtype of the parent's return type (Account → SavingsAccount is valid). (2) ACCESS MODIFIER — can be WIDENED but NOT narrowed (protected → public is OK; public → private is NOT). (3) EXCEPTIONS — checked exceptions can be NARROWED or removed but NOT widened (IOException → FileNotFoundException OK; IOException → Exception NOT OK). Runtime exceptions have no restriction. (4) FINAL/STATIC/PRIVATE — cannot be overridden (final = sealed, static = hidden not overridden, private = not inherited). (5) @Override — annotation that makes the compiler verify the method actually overrides a parent method (catches typos).
s1_definition.analogy: Overriding is like the bank's branch manager REPLACING the head office's default procedure with a local one. Head office says "calculate interest at 3%." Mumbai branch OVERRIDES: "calculate at 4% (city premium)." Rules: the branch CAN make the procedure MORE accessible (if HO says staff-only, branch can make it public), but CANNOT make it MORE restricted (if HO says public, branch can't make it private). The branch CAN narrow the errors (fewer things can go wrong), but CANNOT add NEW errors that HO didn't declare. And if HO marks a procedure FINAL: no branch can change it.
s1_definition.oneliner: Override = same name + same params in child. Return: same or covariant (narrower). Access: same or wider. Checked exceptions: same or narrower. Cannot override: final, static, private. Always use @Override.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Method overriding occurs when a child class provides a SPECIFIC implementation for a method already defined in its parent class. The overriding method must have the SAME name, SAME parameter list, and a COMPATIBLE return type. Five rules govern overriding: (1) COVARIANT RETURN — the return type can be the same OR a subtype of the parent's return type (Account → SavingsAccount is valid). (2) ACCESS MODIFIER — can be WIDENED but NOT narrowed (protected → public is OK; public → private is NOT). (3) EXCEPTIONS — checked exceptions can be NARROWED or removed but NOT widened (IOException → FileNotFoundException OK; IOException → Exception NOT OK). Runtime exceptions have no restriction. (4) FINAL/STATIC/PRIVATE — cannot be overridden (final = sealed, static = hidden not overridden, private = not inherited). (5) @Override — annotation that makes the compiler verify the method actually overrides a parent method (catches typos).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Overriding is like the bank's branch manager REPLACING the head office's default procedure with a local one. Head office says "calculate interest at 3%." Mumbai branch OVERRIDES: "calculate at 4% (city premium)." Rules: the branch CAN make the procedure MORE accessible (if HO says staff-only, branch can make it public), but CANNOT make it MORE restricted (if HO says public, branch can't make it private). The branch CAN narrow the errors (fewer things can go wrong), but CANNOT add NEW errors that HO didn't declare. And if HO marks a procedure FINAL: no branch can change it.

**One line to remember:** Override = same name + same params in child. Return: same or covariant (narrower). Access: same or wider. Checked exceptions: same or narrower. Cannot override: final, static, private. Always use @Override.

sections.s3_banking:
**Problem — The bank's account hierarchy has specific overriding needs.** SavingsAccount overrides `calculateInterest()` with covariant return (returns SavingsInterestResult instead of InterestResult). CurrentAccount overrides `withdraw()` with WIDER access (protected → public — because current accounts allow public API withdrawal). The NRIAccount overrides `loadCompliance()` with NARROWER exception (IOException → FileNotFoundException). A developer tried to override a final method (`getAccountId()`) and a static method (`getBankName()`) — both failed for different reasons. The test suite proves each overriding rule.

**What the project will show:** Covariant return type, access modifier widening, checked exception narrowing, final method blocking, static method hiding (not overriding), @Override catching typos, and Liskov Substitution Principle in action.

sections.s5_journey:
**Step 1 — Covariant return.** Parent `AccountFactory.create()` returns `Account`. Child `SavingsAccountFactory.create()` returns `SavingsAccount`. Through child reference: no cast needed — caller gets SavingsAccount directly. Through parent reference: returns Account (but actual IS SavingsAccount — cast available if needed).

**Step 2 — Access widening.** Parent `Account.processInternal()` is protected. Child `SavingsAccount.processInternal()` is public. Any code that could call it via Account reference can still call it — child is MORE accessible, not less. If child narrowed to private: code calling through Account reference would unexpectedly fail — violates Liskov.

**Step 3 — Exception narrowing.** Parent `loadData()` throws IOException. SavingsAccount narrows to FileNotFoundException. CurrentAccount removes exception entirely. Callers that catch IOException still work — FileNotFoundException IS-A IOException. If child WIDENED to Exception: callers catching IOException would miss it — program crashes.

**Step 4 — Final blocks override.** `getAccountId()` is final — immutable identity. No child can change how accountId is returned. This guarantees: every Account always returns its real ID, regardless of the subclass.

**Step 5 — Static is hidden, not overridden.** `Account ref = new SavingsAccount(...)`. `ref.getBankName()` calls Account.getBankName() — "National Bank of India". NOT SavingsAccount.getBankName(). Static methods bind at compile time to the VARIABLE TYPE, not the actual object type. No dynamic dispatch. This proves static methods are HIDDEN, not overridden.
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ═══ FIVE OVERRIDING RULES ═══

  RULE 1 — COVARIANT RETURN:
    Parent: InterestResult calculateInterest()
    Child:  SavingsInterestResult calculateInterest()  ✅ subtype return
    Invalid: Account calculateInterest() on child of SavingsAccount  ❌ wider return

  RULE 2 — ACCESS MODIFIER:
    Parent: protected processInternal()
    Child:  public processInternal()     ✅ wider access
    Invalid: private processInternal()   ❌ narrower access
    Order: private → default → protected → public (can only move RIGHT)

  RULE 3 — CHECKED EXCEPTIONS:
    Parent: void loadData() throws IOException
    Child:  void loadData() throws FileNotFoundException  ✅ narrower
    Child:  void loadData()                               ✅ removed
    Invalid: void loadData() throws Exception             ❌ wider
    Invalid: void loadData() throws IOException, SQLException  ❌ new exception

  RULE 4 — CANNOT OVERRIDE:
    final method  → COMPILE ERROR (sealed by parent)
    static method → HIDDEN, not overridden (compile-time binding to class)
    private method → NOT inherited (child's same-name method is NEW, not override)

  RULE 5 — @Override:
    With @Override: compiler verifies signature matches parent ✅
    Without: typo creates NEW method silently — BUG! ❌
    Always use @Override. Non-negotiable.
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Method overriding has five rules. First, covariant return types: the child's return type can be a subtype of the parent's return type — SavingsInterestResult instead of InterestResult. This lets callers using the child reference access subtype-specific methods without casting. Second, access modifiers can be widened but not narrowed: protected can become public, but public cannot become private — because callers accessing through the parent reference must still have access. Third, checked exceptions can be narrowed or removed but not widened: IOException can become FileNotFoundException or be removed entirely, but cannot become Exception — because callers catching IOException would miss the wider exception.

In my override-rules service, SavingsAccount demonstrates all three positive rules: covariant return (SavingsInterestResult), wider access (protected → public), and narrower exception (IOException → FileNotFoundException). CurrentAccount demonstrates exception removal (loadData throws nothing). The final keyword on getAccountId prevents any child from changing how the ID is returned — critical for identity fields. Static methods are HIDDEN, not overridden: `Account ref = new SavingsAccount(...)` followed by `ref.getBankName()` returns "National Bank of India" (Account's version), not "Savings Division" — proving static methods bind at compile time to the variable type.

The most important practical rule is @Override: always use it. Without it, a typo like calculateIntrest() (missing 'e') silently creates a new method instead of overriding the parent's calculateInterest(). The parent's version still runs — returning zero interest for savings accounts. With @Override, the compiler immediately reports "method does not override or implement a method from a supertype" — catching the bug before it reaches production.
